Paper_name: Electrophysiological correlates of self-related processing in adults with autism
Summary: This study investigated the temporal course of self-related processing in adults with and without autism using a shape-label matching task while recording event-related potentials (ERPs). The research examined the self-bias effect, which refers to the human tendency to prioritize self- over other-related stimuli. Thirty-two adults with autism and 27 neurotypical controls completed the task while ERPs were recorded. Behavioral results showed comparable self-bias effects across both groups with no differences in task performance.
Author: Letizia Amodeo, Judith Goris, Annabel D. Nijhof, Jan R. Wiersema
Conclusion: The autism group showed a similar self-bias at early stages of processing (N1 component) but demonstrated a lessened differentiation between self- and other-related stimuli at later stages (parietal P3 component). This indicates equivalent self-bias at early sensory stages but strongly diminished self-bias at later cognitive stages in adults with autism, supporting claims that later phases of self-related processing are altered in autism.
